citation: Primary text: Papyrus Bremner-Rhind, British Museum EA 10188 (Papyrus of Nesmin), hieratic, Thebes. Translation: R. O. Faulkner, 'The Bremner-Rhind Papyrus: III. D. The Book of Overthrowing ʿApep', Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 23 (1937), 166-185, and 'The Bremner-Rhind Papyrus: IV', JEA 24 (1938), 41-53 (some bibliographies give 41-52). Faulkner's translation read via Attalus, 'Egyptian Texts 1.4: The Book of Overthrowing Apep', https://www.attalus.org/egypt/apep.html. Museum record: British Museum collection online, EA 10188 sheets, e.g. https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA10188-13.
evidence_tier: Primary source in scholarly translation (Faulkner, peer-reviewed JEA), plus museum record (British Museum collection database).
access_status: Faulkner translation of cols. 22-32 fully read on attalus.org (whole page downloaded and read end to end). British Museum collection page returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch; its content seen only as a search-engine summary. Faulkner's JEA articles themselves (with commentary and notes) not opened; only the Attalus reproduction of the translation and the JSTOR citation header seen in search results.
exact_quotes: Attalus header: 'Text: BM EA 10188 [ TM 48496 ] Date: c. 305 B.C. Script: Hieratic Translated by: R.O. Faulkner'.
Attalus intro: 'The effect of the spells was heightened by the use of red ink in some places, as reproduced here.' and 'The translation is by R.O. Faulkner (JEA, 1937 & 1938).'

Col. 22, opening title: 'Here begins the book of the felling of ʿApep the foe of Rê and the foe of King Onnophris, the justified, which is performed daily in the temple of Amen-Rê, Lord of the Thrones of the Two Lands, who dwells in Karnak.'

Col. 22, spell titles in sequence: 'The spell of spitting on ʿApep.' / 'The spell of trampling on ʿApep with the left foot.' / 'The spell of taking the spear to smite ʿApep.' / 'The spell of binding ʿApep.' / 'The spell of taking the knife to smite ʿApep.' / 'The spell of setting fire to ʿApep.' / 'The magic spell to be uttered when putting ʿApep on the fire.'
Col. 22: 'Pharaoh, he adores Rê and thrusts his spear into ʿApep; he takes a flaming brand and sets fire to him'.
Col. 22: 'this is that head of thine, O ʿApep, which are cut off by the warrior priest with his knife.'
Col. 23: 'Now afterward thou shalt trample on ʿApep four times with thy left foot and thou shalt say before Rê with thine arms bent when he rises:- Rê is triumphant over thee, O ʿApep - four times'.

Col. 23 rubric: 'This spell is to be spoken over a figure of ʿApep drawn on a new sheet of papyrus in green ink, and there shall be made an image of ʿApep with waxen body with his name inscribed on it in green ink, to be put on the fire that he may burn before Rê when he manifests himself in the morning, at noon-tide, and also in the evening when Rê sets in the West; at the sixth hour of the night, at the eighth hour of the day, at the end of the evening, down to every hour of the day and night, at the festival of the new moon, at the day of the monthly festival, at the sixth-day festival, at the fifteenth-day festival, and likewise every day. ʿApep the foe of Rê is felled in storm by the shining of Rê, ʿApep is felled in very truth. He is to be burnt in a fire of bryony and his remains placed in a pot of urine and pounded up into one mass.'

Col. 23 rubric, continued: 'Thou shalt do accordingly at the sixth hour of the night and at the eighth hour of the day, placing ʿApep on the fire and spitting on him very often at the beginning of every hour of the day until the turning of the shadow. After this, at the sixth hour of the day, thou shalt place ʿApep on the fire, spitting on him and trampling on him with thy left foot, and driving off the roarer Nehaher. Thou shalt do accordingly at the eighth hour of the day, driving off ʿApep that he may not attack the Night-bark.'

Col. 23 rubric, storms: 'Thou shalt do accordingly when storm brews in the east of the sky and when Rê sets in the west in order to prevent the storm-red from growing in the east of the sky. Thou shalt do accordingly very often in order to prevent bad weather from growing in the sky and to prevent thunder-storms from growing in the sky. Thou shalt do this very often against storm so that the sun may shine and ʿApep be felled in very truth'.

Col. 23 rubric, benefit and testimony: 'it will be well with whoso does it upon earth, and it will be well with him in the realm of the dead, strength shall be given to that man to attain the office of his superior, and it will be his salvation from all evil and harmful things in very truth; I have seen it come to pass in mine own case.'

Col. 24 (end of first book): 'Thou shalt nevermore come forth from this thine hell.' and 'the Eye of Rê shall have power over thee and it shall consume thee every day, even as Rê commanded should be done to thee'.

Col. 24 rubric: 'To be recited by a man who is pure and clean. Thou shalt depict (?) the name of ʿApep, it being written on a new sheet of papyrus, and it shall be put in the fire when Rê manifests himself, when Rê is at noon-tide, when Rê sets in the West, by night, by day, at every hour of every day, at the monthly festival, at the sixth-day festival, at the fifteenth-day festival, and likewise every day when the foes of Rê-Harakhti are felled.'

Col. 26 rubric (foes of Pharaoh): 'To be recited by a man who is pure and clean. Thou shalt depict (?) every foe of Rê and every foe of Pharaoh, whether dead or alive, and every accused one whom he has in mind, also the names of their fathers, their mothers and their children, every one of them (?), they having been drawn in green ink on a new sheet of papyrus, their names written on their breasts, these having been made of wax, and also bound with bonds (?) of black thread; they are to be spat upon, and they are to be trampled with the left foot, felled with the spear and knife, and cast on the fire in the melting-furnace of the coppersmiths. Afterwards, the name of ʿApep is to be burnt in a fire of bryony when Rê manifests himself, when Rê is at noontide, and when Rê sets in the West; in the first hour of the day and of the night and in the second hour of the night down to the third hour of the night; at dawn, and likewise every hour of the night and every hour of the day'.
Col. 26, end of rubric: 'It will be well with the man who makes conjuration for himself from this book in the presence of this august god-a true matter, tested a million times.'

Col. 26 rubric (morning book): 'To be recited over an image of ʿApep made with a waxen body and also drawn on a new sheet of papyrus; to be put on the fire before Rê every day, and likewise on the day of the monthly festival and the days of the sixth-day festival and the fifteenth-day festival, in order to fell ʿApep on water, land, and river-bank.'

Col. 28 rubric: 'This spell is to be spoken over a figure of ʿApep drawn upon a new sheet of papyrus in green ink and placed within a box (?) with his name indicated upon it, he being bound and fettered, to be put on the fire every day, trampled with thy left foot and spat upon four times daily.'

Col. 28 rubric, continued: 'they are to be made (?) in wax, put on the fire after the name of ʿApep, and burnt when Rê manifests himself; thou shalt do the like of? the first time at the middle of the day and when Rê sets in the West, when the sunlight flees to the mountain. This shall be better for thee than any other act in very truth'.

Col. 29 rubric: 'To be recited over an image of ʿApep made of wax with his name written on it in green ink; he shall also be made on a new sheet of papyrus, and the images of all the foes of Pharaoh, dead or alive, shall also be made in wax, and their names written on them in green ink, they being bound within a box (?); they shall be spat upon and trampled with thy left foot, slaughtered with a knife, put on a fire of bryony and quenched with the urine of a ... woman. And the names of ʿApep and of all the foes of Pharaoh, dead or alive, are to be written in pigment (?) on the ground, and trampled with thy left foot in the correct manner.'
Col. 29: 'It is a secret book of the House of Life (?), which none see; the secret book of felling ʿApep.'
Col. 29: 'So is he to be felled and his power of movement taken away, that he may not attack the Night-bark; the knife is given power over him daily in the presence of Rê'.
Col. 31: 'Thy head shall be cut off with this knife in the presence of Rê every day'.
Col. 32: 'Shu thrusts his spear into thee, and thou shalt submerge and not emerge again, O ʿApep thou foe of Rê. Be thou spat upon, O ʿApep - four times'.
Col. 32, final rubric: 'This spell is to be spoken when Rê is upon the hill of the Lake of Desdes in order to rejuvenate the king with life; its name is The Book of the Lord of All. It is at an end.'

British Museum record (via search summary, not opened directly): Papyrus of Nesmin; production date '305 BC (acc. to colophon)'; findspot Thebes; 'Book of Overthrowing Apep' is 'cols 22-32'; 'Names of Apep' cols 32-33; 'Songs of Isis and Nephthys' cols 1-17; 'Ritual of Bringing in Sokar' cols 18-21; acquired 1865 [uncertain].
date_and_recency: Translation published 1937 (JEA 23) and 1938 (JEA 24); Attalus web edition undated, accessed 2026-11-28. Manuscript dated c. 305 BC (British Museum: '305 BC (acc. to colophon)'), early Ptolemaic period; the text it copies is older but its date of composition is not stated in the opened sources.
key_claims: The book's own title says it 'is performed daily in the temple of Amen-Rê, Lord of the Thrones of the Two Lands, who dwells in Karnak' (col. 22).
The opening sequence is a set of named actions on ʿApep: spitting, trampling with the left foot, spearing, binding, the knife, setting fire, and putting on the fire (col. 22).
The figure of ʿApep is drawn 'on a new sheet of papyrus in green ink'; a wax image is also made 'with his name inscribed on it in green ink' and burnt (col. 23; repeated cols. 26, 28, 29).

The rite is tied to set times: morning, noon and sunset; the sixth hour of the night and the eighth hour of the day; 'every hour of the day and night'; the new-moon, monthly, sixth-day and fifteenth-day festivals; 'and likewise every day' (col. 23, col. 24, col. 26).

It is also to be done against weather: 'when storm brews in the east of the sky', 'to prevent bad weather', 'to prevent thunder-storms', 'very often against storm so that the sun may shine' (col. 23).
The remains are burnt 'in a fire of bryony', placed 'in a pot of urine and pounded up into one mass' (col. 23); in col. 29 the wax figures are 'quenched with the urine of a ... woman'.

The rite extends to human enemies: wax figures of 'every foe of Rê and every foe of Pharaoh, whether dead or alive', with names of their parents and children, bound 'with bonds (?) of black thread', spat on, trampled, 'felled with the spear and knife', and 'cast on the fire in the melting-furnace of the coppersmiths' (col. 26).
The officiant must be 'a man who is pure and clean' (cols. 24, 26); the text speaks of a 'warrior priest' cutting off the heads with his knife (col. 22).
The text claims efficacy for the practitioner, in this life and after death: 'I have seen it come to pass in mine own case' (col. 23); 'a true matter, tested a million times' (col. 26).
It calls itself 'a secret book of the House of Life (?), which none see' (col. 29).
The British Museum identifies the papyrus as belonging to Nesmin, dated 305 BC by its colophon, from Thebes, with the Apep book at cols. 22-32 [uncertain: from search summary of the museum page].
headline_figures: Columns: Book of Overthrowing Apep occupies cols. 22-32 of BM EA 10188 (British Museum, via search summary; Attalus text runs [22] to [32]).
Date: 'c. 305 B.C.' (Attalus header); '305 BC (acc. to colophon)' (British Museum, via search summary).
'four times': trampling 'four times with thy left foot' (col. 23); 'spat upon four times daily' (col. 28); many refrains marked '- four times -'.

Hours named: 'the sixth hour of the night', 'the eighth hour of the day' (col. 23); 'the sixth hour of the day' (col. 23); 'the first hour of the day and of the night and in the second hour of the night down to the third hour of the night' (col. 26).
Festivals named: new moon, 'monthly festival', 'sixth-day festival', 'fifteenth-day festival' (cols. 23, 24, 26).
Three daily solar stations: 'in the morning, at noon-tide, and also in the evening when Rê sets in the West' (col. 23).
'tested a million times' (col. 26), a formula claim, not a count.
Faulkner citation: JEA 23 (1937) 166-185 (Part III); JEA 24 (1938) 41-53 (Part IV; TLA gives 41-52).
dating_and_context: Hieratic manuscript, BM EA 10188, from Thebes, dated by its colophon to 305 BC (British Museum, seen via search summary). The same roll also holds the Songs of Isis and Nephthys (cols. 1-17) and the Ritual of Bringing in Sokar (cols. 18-21), and the Names of Apep follow at cols. 32-33. Owner named by the museum as Nesmin (Budge's older Archaeologia publication renders the name 'Nesi-Amsu, a scribe in the temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes, about B.C. 305', seen only as a search result title). Purchased by the museum in 1865 (from David Bremner; previous owner Alexander Henry Rhind) [uncertain: that detail was shown for sister item EA 10208,3, not confirmed for EA 10188].
what_it_says_about_apophis: ʿApep is 'the foe of Rê', a serpent 'who hast neither arms nor legs', who threatens the sun-bark; the rites are done 'that he may not attack the Night-bark' (cols. 23, 29). Each spell declares him destroyed in absolute terms: 'Thou shalt nevermore come forth from this thine hell' (col. 24); 'thou shalt submerge and not emerge again' (col. 32); 'Rê has felled thee for ever' (col. 30). Yet the same text has the destruction repeat without end: 'the Eye of Rê shall have power over thee and it shall consume thee every day' (col. 24); 'thou art given over to the fire every day as Rê commanded' (col. 28); 'Thy head shall be cut off with this knife in the presence of Rê every day' (col. 31); 'the knife shall be stuck fast in his head in the presence of Rê every day' (col. 27). Storms and the 'storm-red' in the eastern sky are treated as ʿApep's activity, answered by the rite 'so that the sun may shine' (col. 23). He is also defeated within the creation account (cols. 26-29), where the creator's offspring 'created the magic spells for felling ʿApep'. In this text chaos is declared beaten in every spell and has to be beaten again every day.
ritual_practice: In the temple of Amun-Ra at Karnak (col. 22 title), a man 'pure and clean' (cols. 24, 26) recites the spells over a figure of ʿApep drawn on a new sheet of papyrus in green ink and a wax image with his name written on it in green ink. The figure is spat on, trampled with the left foot (four times), speared, bound, cut with a knife by the 'warrior priest', and burnt in a fire of bryony; the remains go into a pot of urine and are pounded into one mass (col. 23), or the figures are quenched with a woman's urine (col. 29). At sunrise the officiant tramples ʿApep four times and speaks 'before Rê with thine arms bent when he rises'. A variant puts the drawn figure 'within a box (?)', bound and fettered (col. 28). Wax figures of the king's human enemies, living or dead, with names of their parents and children on their breasts, bound with black thread, are treated the same way and thrown into 'the melting-furnace of the coppersmiths' (col. 26). The names of ʿApep and the king's foes are also written 'in pigment (?) on the ground' and trampled (col. 29). The book is also used 'when the sacred bark ferries over' at Yat-Pega (col. 26).
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Prescribed: 'daily' (title, col. 22); at morning, noon and sunset; at the sixth hour of the night and eighth hour of the day; at 'the beginning of every hour of the day until the turning of the shadow'; 'down to every hour of the day and night'; at the new-moon, monthly, sixth-day and fifteenth-day festivals; and 'very often' whenever storm threatens (col. 23). 'spat upon four times daily' (col. 28). Attested: this source is a liturgical manuscript and gives prescriptions, not a record of performance. The only claims of actual use are formulaic: 'I have seen it come to pass in mine own case' (col. 23) and 'tested a million times' (col. 26). Nothing opened for this item shows how often the rite was in fact done at Karnak, and Faulkner's commentary (not opened) may discuss it [uncertain].
relevance_to_angle: Strong support. The book is framed as a daily temple service, scheduled by hour and festival, and extended to an on-demand response whenever storm clouds gather. Every spell proclaims final, total destruction ('nevermore', 'for ever and ever'), but the rubrics tell the priest to do it again tomorrow, at the next hour, at the next storm. That gap between the rhetoric of final victory and the practice of endless repetition is the routine-maintenance reading in the text's own words. The complication: the language is triumphalist, not resigned. The text never says chaos cannot be defeated; it keeps claiming it has been, and its 'every day' can be read either as maintenance or as a cosmic re-enactment of one victory.
limitations_stated: Faulkner marks doubtful renderings with '(?)' throughout, including at load-bearing points: 'Thou shalt depict (?) the name of ʿApep', 'bonds (?) of black thread', 'within a box (?)', 'written in pigment (?) on the ground', 'House of Life (?)', and the lacuna 'the urine of a ... woman'. Col. 28 contains a garbled phrase, 'thou shalt do the like of? the first time at the middle of the day'. Attalus notes it reproduces red ink 'in some places', i.e. the rubrics, but the plain-text extraction used here does not show which words were red. Faulkner's footnotes and commentary in JEA were not opened.
source_discrepancies: Ink colour: Faulkner consistently has the figure and names drawn 'in green ink'; popular retellings often say ʿApep's name was written in red ink. The red in the papyrus is the scribe's rubric ink (Attalus: 'use of red ink in some places'), which is a separate matter from the ink the rubrics prescribe for the figure [uncertain whether any translator renders the prescribed ink differently; not checked]. Faulkner citation: the search summary of the BM page cited Faulkner JEA 22 (1936) 121-40, which is Part I (Songs of Isis and Nephthys), not the Apep book; the Apep translation is Part III, JEA 23 (1937) 166-185, and Part IV, JEA 24 (1938) 41-53 or 41-52 depending on bibliography. Column ranges: BM lists Apep book as cols. 22-32 and Names of Apep as cols. 32-33; Attalus text ends at col. 32 with 'It is at an end', so the Names of Apep list is not in the Attalus page. Owner name: 'Nesmin' (BM) vs 'Nesi-Amsu' (Budge, older reading of the same name) [uncertain: equivalence inferred from matching date and temple title].
verification_status: Checked against Faulkner's translation actually opened (attalus.org, full text read): the col. 22 title (daily, Karnak), the spell sequence, all rubric quotations on green ink, wax, new papyrus, bryony, urine, black thread, coppersmiths' furnace, hours, festivals, storms, the 'pure and clean' officiant, 'warrior priest', 'secret book of the House of Life (?)', 'I have seen it come to pass in mine own case', 'tested a million times'. Not checked against an opened primary page [uncertain]: British Museum record details (owner Nesmin, '305 BC (acc. to colophon)', Thebes findspot, column ranges, 1865 acquisition), because the BM page returned 403 and was seen only via a search summary; Faulkner JEA page ranges (from search results and JSTOR header snippet, not the article itself); Budge's 'Nesi-Amsu' title (search result title only). The hieratic original and Faulkner's own commentary were not consulted.
